title: Explore NASA's InSight Mission on Mars
byline: The New York Times · Augmented Reality · 2018

contentUnits.title: Beat 1
contentUnits.text: THE INSIGHT LANDER is NASA's newest mission to Mars, set to land on Nov. 26, 2018. It will study the deep structure of the planet.

contentUnits.title: Beat 2
contentUnits.text: THE CURIOSITY ROVER has been exploring and drilling in Gale Crater since 2012.

contentUnits.title: Beat 3
contentUnits.text: THE PHOENIX LANDER touched down near Mars' north pole in 2008, and found water ice under the surface.

contentUnits.title: Beat 4
contentUnits.text: THE OPPORTUNITY ROVER roamed Mars from 2004 until a 2018 dust storm obscured its solar panels and cut its power.

contentUnits.title: Beat 5
contentUnits.text: THE SPIRIT ROVER roamed Mars from 2004 to 2009, when it became stuck in a patch of soft ground.

contentUnits.title: Beat 6
contentUnits.text: THE PATHFINDER MISSION landed in 1997 and carried Sojourner, the first Martian rover.

contentUnits.title: Beat 7
contentUnits.text: THE VIKING LANDERS, 1 and 2, both carried seismometers in the 1970s but were unable to definitively detect marsquakes.

contentUnits.title: Beat 8
contentUnits.text: EARLY MARS. An artist's conception of the young planet, before its water was lost to space or froze into the ground.

contentUnits.title: Beat 9
contentUnits.text: INSIGHT ON THE SURFACE. Unlike the rovers, InSight stays put — a stationary platform built to listen to the planet itself.

contentUnits.title: Beat 10
contentUnits.text: SEISMOMETER (SEIS). Lowered to the ground under a chainmail-skirted dome, it detects vibrations from marsquakes and meteorite impacts.

contentUnits.title: Beat 11
contentUnits.text: HEAT FLOW PROBE (HP³). A self-hammering probe drives about 16 feet into the soil to measure heat welling up from the planet's core.

contentUnits.title: Beat 12
contentUnits.text: RADIO EXPERIMENT (RISE). Antennas on the deck let Earth track how Mars wobbles as it orbits the sun, revealing the size of its core.
